title: Front vs. Back of the Conscious Cortex: Higher-Order Thought & Reality Monitoring vs. Local Recurrent Processing — Blindsight discrimination without seeing & Sperling's 12-letter iconic overflow; Lamme's 4-stage V1 feedforward (<80 ms) vs recurrent figure-ground (~100 ms) physiology; Lau & Passingham's matched-d' BA 46 relative blindsight & LeDoux-Brown's HOROR split between amygdala survival reflexes and conscious fear; Tsuchiya's no-report OKN/pupil rivalry, Boly vs Odegaard-Knight-Lau's 2017 frontal-lesion duel & Ferrante's N=256 Cogitate Nature test; SDT d' vs meta-d' M-ratio math, Sperling bit budgets & 7T laminar + tFUS TOST equivalence protocols

teenKit.tldr: Your brain can process complex information and react to it perfectly without you ever consciously seeing or experiencing it. Consciousness isn't just about your senses working; it's a separate mental spotlight deciding what you actually notice.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding the gap between brain activity and conscious awareness changes how we treat brain injuries, understand mental health, and decode what it actually means to be "aware."
keyTakeaways: Blindsight proves your eyes and brain can track movement and details accurately while your conscious mind sees total darkness.
George Sperling's 1960 experiment showed our brains briefly hold a massive sensory snapshot that vanishes before we can name everything we saw.
Neuroscientists are locked in a high-stakes debate over whether consciousness happens locally in sensory areas or globally via the frontal cortex.

vocab.meaning: A rare condition where people with damaged primary visual cortexes can accurately guess details about objects they swear they cannot see.
The theory that sensory input only becomes conscious when higher brain regions in the prefrontal cortex scan and evaluate it.
The rival theory that consciousness emerges quickly through feedback loops right inside local sensory areas like the visual cortex, without needing the front of the brain.
The phenomenon where your senses briefly capture a massive amount of visual data, but your conscious working memory can only grab a tiny fraction of it.

quiz.question: In the blindsight experiment from the podcast, what happens when a patient is asked to guess the direction of a moving bar in their blind spot?
options: They freeze up and refuse to answer because they see nothing.
They guess correctly 85 to 95 percent of the time while still claiming they see pure blackness.
They accurately describe the color, shape, and speed of the bar.
Their brain activity completely flatlines until the stimulus is removed.
quiz.explanation: Patients with blindsight achieve high objective accuracy through unconscious processing despite having zero subjective experience of seeing the bar.

quiz.question: What did George Sperling's 1960 grid of 12 letters reveal about human perception?
options: People can consciously read and remember all 12 letters perfectly if given 50 milliseconds.
The human eye cannot process uppercase letters when flashed rapidly.
People feel like they saw all 12 letters at once, but the image fades before they can name more than a few.
Working memory can hold an infinite amount of visual data if it is flashed quickly enough.
quiz.explanation: Participants experience a vivid iconic memory of all 12 items, but it vanishes before they have time to articulate more than a fraction of them.

quiz.question: What is the core disagreement between Higher-Order Thought (HOT) theories and Local Recurrent Processing theories?
options: Whether the left hemisphere is completely inactive during visual tasks.
Whether consciousness requires involvement from the front of the brain or just local loops in sensory areas.
Whether animals possess any form of visual processing.
Whether light actually enters the retina before the brain begins processing it.
quiz.explanation: The great debate centers on whether consciousness demands high-level prefrontal evaluation or sparks instantly from feedback loops inside sensory cortices.
